title: How Ancient Potato Farming May Have Rewired Andean DNA
summary: For thousands of years, potatoes have been the backbone of Andean diets. Now, scientists have uncovered evidence that this humble tuber may have literally shaped human evolution. A new study published in Nature Communications finds that Indigenous Quechua speakers in the Peruvian Andes possess the highest known number of copies of the salivary amylase gene, AMY1. This gene codes for an enzyme that kick-starts starch digestion in the mouth. People with more copies tend to produce more amylase, making them more efficient at breaking down starchy foods like potatoes. The research, co-led by UCLA and the University at Buffalo, suggests that natural selection began favoring individuals with extra AMY1 copies around the same time potatoes were domesticated in the highlands, roughly 6,000 to 10,000 years ago. "Evolution is chiseling a sculpture, not constructing a building," explained co-corresponding author Omer Gokcumen. Rather than gaining new copies, those with fewer copies were gradually eliminated from the gene pool over generations. Today, Indigenous Peruvians average 10 AMY1 copies—two to four more than any of the other 83 populations examined. To rule out other factors, the team compared them with the Maya, a genetically related group in Mexico that did not historically rely on potatoes. The Maya averaged just 6 copies. The researchers also accounted for the catastrophic population bottleneck following European contact, which could have randomly reduced genetic diversity. Their analysis confirmed that potato farming, not random drift, was the primary driver. "There are very few cases where the evidence for diet-driven natural selection is this strong," Gokcumen noted. This discovery highlights how the Andes—already famous for adaptations to high-altitude hypoxia—continue to reveal how human populations evolve in response to their environment. It's a powerful reminder that what we eat can, over millennia, leave a lasting mark on our DNA.
why_it_matters: This research shows that what people have eaten for thousands of years can leave a permanent mark on their DNA — a powerful example of culture shaping biology. As global diets change rapidly, understanding how our genes and food interact could help us anticipate future health challenges related to starch digestion and nutrition.

background_read: Potatoes were first domesticated in the high Andes of Peru and Bolivia roughly 8,000 years ago, making them one of the world's oldest staple crops. The tubers are rich in starch, a complex carbohydrate that requires the enzyme amylase to be broken down into simple sugars.

Humans have several copies of the AMY1 gene, but the number can vary widely between individuals and populations. People with more copies tend to produce more salivary amylase, which jump-starts digestion the moment starchy food enters the mouth. Other well-known examples of diet-driven genetic adaptations include the ability to digest milk sugar (lactose) into adulthood among pastoralist groups in Europe and Africa.

The Quechua people, descendants of the Inca, have long depended on potatoes at altitudes where few other crops thrive. This study, published in Nature Communications (a top scientific journal), is co-led by researchers from UCLA and the University at Buffalo, and it builds on earlier discoveries that Andeans also have genetic traits helping them survive low oxygen levels.

perspectives.description: Archaeologists and geneticists see this as a landmark example of gene-culture coevolution. It validates the ingenuity of ancient Andean farmers who domesticated the potato, a food that not only sustained them but literally sculpted their descendants' genes. Indigenous communities may also view this as scientific recognition of their agricultural heritage.

Historical context is sobering: the population bottleneck mentioned in the study was caused by European colonization, which led to massive loss of life among Indigenous Peruvians. Some critics worry that genetic research on Indigenous groups, even well-intentioned, can oversimplify complex histories or be used without proper community consent.

Strong diet-gene linkages are rare because many factors shape the human genome. This Andean case parallels the evolution of lactase persistence in herding societies, but it stands out because the signal survived a severe population crash — making the evidence unusually robust. It raises the question: what other diet-driven adaptations might be hidden in human genomes?

Knowing that extra amylase genes improve starch digestion could influence personalized nutrition in the future. As scientists map diverse genomes worldwide, they may find more such relationships, helping doctors tailor diets to people's genetic makeup. The Andes, already a treasure trove of evolutionary adaptations, will likely keep revealing how environment shapes our species.
